title: What Changes When Data Center Sustainability Becomes Comparable?
excerpt: On 21 September, the European Commission adopted a new rating scheme for data centres to label their sustainability.
html:
On 21 September, the European Commission adopted a new rating scheme for data centres to label their sustainability.

The industry was already reporting on sustainability metrics. What has changed is how that information can be used. The new scheme sets a framework which helps compare data centres.

This shift creates new pressure for operators.

Reporting sustainability performance has always been part of the process, this is now combined with classifying and comparing the performance of facilities.

So what changes when the market can directly compare data centre sustainability?

What does the new rating actually change?

The scheme uses information that data centres already report, making it easier to compare facilities, focusing on PUE and WUE.

PUE stands for Power Usage Effectiveness. In short, it compares how much energy enters the data centre with how much reaches the IT equipment.

WUE, on the other hand, is similar. It measures usage effectiveness for water rather than power, showing how much is used relative to the computing work it supports.

The label also provides context on the energy source, local conditions, whether waste heat can be reused, and how the facility interacts with the grid, making weaker areas easier to identify.

For example, a business could have a good PUE and a terrible WUE. This would show that while energy use is efficient, freshwater use is poor.

This also gives operators a clearer view of where they perform well and where they fall behind.

As a result, the question shifts from whether an operator reports the right information to how facilities perform compared with others.

Why isn’t improving sustainability as simple as improving the score?

A weaker score is visible, but it does not reveal the reason behind it.

Data centres don’t exist in identical settings. Conditions can vary depending on climate, water availability, cooling systems, facility age, utilisation and existing infrastructure.

Sometimes, trade-offs are made.

Reducing energy use can affect water consumption, and some facilities may be limited in where they can improve because of their current design and infrastructure.

Most importantly, improving sustainability cannot come at the expense of keeping a facility operational. While the label provides context, it can’t offer a concrete solution.

Once a weakness is identified, the next step is to identify the cause and evaluate realistic options to move forward.

When does sustainability become an operational decision?

If a facility uses a lot of water, operators may upgrade cooling systems or incorporate recycled water. Improving energy performance could mean adopting advanced power management or increasing the share of renewable electricity.

Other steps might entail optimising airflow, modernising equipment, or investing in heat recovery. The approach itself depends on each facility’s specific circumstances and operations.

Improving sustainability can require changes to equipment, infrastructure and day-to-day operations. These changes require investment and careful planning, and must be carried out without affecting reliability in a live environment.

Consequently, no single team makes these sustainability decisions.

Engineering assesses what can be changed from a technical point of view, operations examines the effect on daily performance, procurement secures the required equipment, and finance considers whether the expected benefits justify the investment.

The European Commission is also considering introducing future minimum-performance standards for data centres, which could put greater pressure on operators to address poor performance rather than merely report it.

When sustainability starts to shape investment decisions and day-to-day operations, the findings move beyond a report and into actions that need to be taken.

What does this change about the people responsible for sustainability?

Anyone involved in sustainability should still understand reporting, regulation and how the business presents its performance.

Yet if the aim is to improve those results, they also need to understand what is causing them.

That does not mean becoming an engineer. It means knowing enough about energy and water use, cooling, renewable power, waste heat and how the facility operates to work properly with the people responsible for those areas.

Consequently, two individuals may have senior experience in sustainability yet come from completely different backgrounds.

One may have spent more time focused on reporting and regulation. Another may have worked far more directly with engineers, operations teams and project delivery, gaining a better understanding of how a data centre actually performs.

One background is not automatically superior, and once sustainability becomes easier to compare, people who can interpret figures and work with the wider business to decide what changes need to be made become more valuable.

Making sustainability comparable does not improve a data centre on its own. It makes the difference between reporting performance and actually managing it much harder to ignore.

title: What Happens When Junior Architecture Pay Rises Faster Than Leadership Pay?
excerpt: The career ladder in architecture is pretty clear. Experience translates to more responsibility, client exposure and more influence over projects and the wider firm.
html:
The career ladder in architecture is pretty clear. Experience translates to more responsibility, client exposure and more influence over projects and the wider firm.

Career growth often equates to salary growth, but salary growth doesn't always increase evenly.

What happens when starting salaries for junior roles begin to grow faster than leadership pay?

What happens to progression when responsibility continues to increase, but the financial difference between levels grows more slowly?

What does salary compression look like?

This isn’t just a theoretical problem. The gap is already narrowing.

The AIA's 2025 Compensation & Benefits Report, having looked at more than 13,000 positions at 817 architecture firms in the United States, shows that early-career architectural staff saw salary increases of around 7% between 2023 and 2025. By comparison, the salaries of firm leaders either stayed the same or went down. This difference is already altering the way the industry compensates its employees.

Take a simple example: juniors start at $60k, seniors at $100k. Then the market shifts. Suddenly, juniors are on $68k, seniors inch up to $101k. The difference is still there, but the gap between the two levels has shrunk from $40k to $33k.

Let this play out a few more times, and it’s not hard to see why senior staff start to wonder: I’m managing people, juggling clients, carrying the can when things go wrong… yet the person two desks down is closing the gap faster than I’d expected.

What would occur then if the pay gap continues to narrow while workloads and responsibilities continue to increase?

What happens to the value of progression?

The higher architects rise in their careers, the less their role is limited to carrying out their own tasks.

Senior roles involve managing clients, budgets, deadlines, and teams. In leadership, you also hire people, look for new projects, maintain relationships, and help run the firm.

So, it’s not a question of whether leaders still earn more.

They do.

The real issue is whether the pay gap matches the extra work leaders take on.

If junior salaries rise quickly while leadership pay barely moves, you can end up with someone taking on a lot more work, but not seeing much extra for it. That doesn’t mean people stop wanting promotions. Progression still brings influence, autonomy, better projects, status, and opportunities that go beyond the payslip.

But the more you ask someone to carry, the more it matters that the next step up actually feels worth it.

Why can junior pay move faster?

The main factor is market rate. What a firm needs to pay to attract someone into the role.

If a practice historically paid graduates $60,000, but competing firms now offer closer to $68,000, it may have to raise its starting salary to stay competitive.

That can quickly raise the entry point of the salary ladder, while people already inside the firm may still sit within an older pay structure.

Suddenly, someone with several years of experience can find themselves only slightly ahead of a new starter.

This creates another question for firms.

If you move the bottom salary band, do you then have to move the ones above it too?

Why can’t firms just increase everyone’s pay?

It may seem like the solution, but it’s not something that can be done in an instant.

Architecture firms can’t just magic money out of thin air to raise salaries.

They have to make the numbers work.

Operating a professional-service business means a large portion of what they sell is their people’s time and expertise.

If salaries rise significantly but client fees don’t keep pace, the firm’s margins get squeezed.

That becomes harder in a weaker market.

AIA reported that architecture compensation growth slowed to less than 3% annually between 2023 and 2025 as staffing shortages eased and wider construction pressures reduced demand.

So moving one salary band can create pressure further up the ladder, but simply increasing everyone’s pay is not always realistic.

Which leaves firms balancing two problems at once.

Keeping salaries competitive enough to attract and retain people, without sacrificing the business's economics.

What does this mean for retention and future leadership?

What experienced staff provide is not just the work they carry out.

They know the clients, the projects, the systems, the teams, the sectors. If their pay slips behind the market, another firm could offer just enough to take all that knowledge with them.

Losing experienced staff can cost much more than the pay raise you wanted to avoid.

You might have to make a counteroffer, reshuffle projects, promote someone who is not ready, or go back to the market and pay the standard rate anyway.

This leads to the bigger issue of succession.

Firms need more than enough architects for today. They need today’s juniors to become tomorrow’s seniors and, eventually, directors.

If responsibility keeps growing but the financial reward shrinks, firms need to consider how attractive the next step up really is.

Holding salaries down might save money now, but replacing experience can cost more later. At that point, it’s less about what someone costs today and more about what it costs if they walk out the door.

In the end, if you want people to take on more as they move up, the pay structure needs to match the career path you want them to follow.

title: What Is Colocation and How Does It Work?
excerpt: As demand for digital infrastructure has surged, the value of data centers has followed.
html:
As demand for digital infrastructure has surged, the value of data centers has followed.

Not every business has the capacity or need to build their own gargantuan structures, so what's the alternative?

Colocation data centers. These structures offer companies a different way to manage their IT infrastructure without needing to operate facilities themselves.

Instead of owning the building, a business can place its own servers and equipment within a specialist center operated by a third party. They provide the infrastructure, meaning the power, cooling, connectivity and physical security, giving the company fewer headaches.

Simply put, the company maintains control of its technology. It just relies on someone else to provide and operate the environment around it.

How it works

Of course, while not every business requires its own data centers, it may still require more space than others. This is a benefit of these spaces.

Customers can rent space variable to their needs. For some, they may only require a small number of racks or a small cage. Whereas, larger companies may need much more dedicated space, power, and infrastructure.

Fortunately, even despite having differing needs, multiple customers can operate inside the same data center. Making the options broader than being confined to their situations.

This is where different forms of colocation can help provide solutions:

Retail Colocation

This is better suited to those with smaller needs. Businesses can rent individual racks, cabinets, cages or smaller areas depending on how much equipment they need to house. This offers flexibility without requiring a company to commit to a huge amount of space.

Wholesale Colocation

Those with more significant requirements may find this is the most suitable solution. Rather than renting a small number of racks, customers may take substantial amounts of space and power, sometimes across large dedicated areas of a facility.

Hybrid Cloud-Based Colocation

Sometimes, physical space isn’t the priority and more so about how the colocation fits into the company's wider strategy. A business might keep some infrastructure in its own environment, place other equipment in a colocation facility and connect that with cloud services.

Why do companies choose colocation?

Data centers are huge commitments: the costs, along with the responsibility, infrastructure and people needed. A lot more is needed to keep these facilities running, beyond what the building is required for.

As obvious as it is, not every business has the means to do so, which is why the colocation model is so attractive. Businesses access the infrastructure without having to build and manage it on their own accord.

This also means a business isn’t bound by its current position. Growth is easier. If a company needs more capacity, it can easily expand within the same facility rather than starting from scratch in a new facility.

On top of this, businesses retain ownership and control of their own hardware. If needs change, they retain their hardware. They’re outsourcing the environment, not necessarily the technology itself.

That is what makes colocation more than simply renting space.

Adapting to New Infrastructure Demands

The proposition of colocation may have started simply as providing businesses with the space and infrastructure needed to house their equipment. However, the pace of change in the industry is accelerating. Power requirements per rack and demands on cooling systems continue to rise.

According to McKinsey, global data center demand is projected to increase from approximately 82 GW in 2025 to 220 GW by 2030, with AI as a significant driver.

For providers, that means supporting customers whose needs look nothing like what the original blueprints imagined. More space isn’t always the answer. The real challenge is making sure the power, cooling and systems can handle what’s inside the facility.

Colocation sites have to be capable of adapting as customer requirements change, whether that means adding capacity, upgrading cooling systems or introducing new infrastructure.

For existing facilities, this can become complex. Changes may need to take place while other customers are already operating inside the data center, without disrupting the services already being provided.

New infrastructure also has to work alongside what is already there. Systems need to be integrated, tested and commissioned to make sure the wider facility can continue operating as intended.

At the same time, colocation is no longer just a place to park physical equipment. It’s part of a bigger cloud and hybrid strategy. Planning a facility now means thinking far beyond how much floor space can be rented.

title: What Makes an Office Building Suitable for Residential Conversion?
excerpt: The ever-increasing demand for housing in New York remains a hot topic.
html:
The ever-increasing demand for housing in New York remains a hot topic.

And this demand isn’t being ignored.

Now, as is almost common knowledge, New York City is a major business hub. It’s the city that never sleeps. Businesses come and go, often leaving offices unused and empty.

This potential had already been explored. By the first quarter of 2025, 44 completed, ongoing or potential office-to-residential conversions had been identified across the city, covering 15.2 million gross square feet.

Empty space? Housing solution.

Possibly, but it’s not that simple.

Office buildings cannot simply be divided into apartments. Each building already has an established shape, structure, windows, utilities, and layout. That doesn’t guarantee these features will automatically translate into what’s needed, but they provide a basis for what needs to be done.

So what do architects and developers need to consider?

Starting With the Existing Building

Obviously, when given a blank slate, there is much more freedom.

You know what’s needed and you can build with that in mind.

But when the building already exists? There’s much more to consider.

Key factors include the existing floor plate, elevator and stairwell placement, and window access.

The building's systems and safety requirements, including plumbing and egress, must also support residential use while staying within zoning and building-law requirements, as these can dramatically change what is possible.

The brief needs to consider that while some parts of the building may be usable, others require alteration or even replacement.

In New York, the question of whether a building can become housing comes down to three things: physical, regulatory, and commercial considerations.

Floor Plates and Natural Light

Offices and homes are built for different lives, often reflected in how these buildings are structured.

Commercial buildings can be deep and wide, designed to pack in desks and meeting rooms, using open space, as people do not necessarily need to live around the edge of the building.

It’s a place to work, not to live.

So when you try to turn workspace into living space, the problems show up quickly.

Apartments need bedrooms, living rooms, and access to natural window light. Where the windows are already set could decide where you can put a bedroom or a kitchen.

The further you get from the edge, the harder it is to make the space work.

At 25 Water Street in Lower Manhattan, two 1,200-square-foot light wells were added to address this challenge, bringing light and air into apartments built within the building’s deep floor plates.

Changing How the Building Works

You can decide on the layout, but that can’t be set in stone unless it works with the systems.

Offices aren’t built for the individual or the family. They’re designed around the workforce.

Plumbing illustrates this challenge clearly. In an office, bathrooms are shared spaces, grouped together. In apartments, kitchens and bathrooms are spread across the floor. Water supply and drainage therefore need to reach places they were never originally designed to serve.

Heating and ventilation systems, originally designed for large open areas, must be reconfigured to support multiple enclosed residential units.

Electrical systems, fire protection and other services also have to accommodate how the building will now be occupied.

Suddenly, systems that work perfectly well for an office don’t translate as simply as assumed.

Safety, Access and Regulation

Regulatory compliance for office use does not automatically extend to residential conversion. The building's purpose has changed, so the housing must meet new standards for fire safety, escape routes, accessibility, and ventilation.

In New York City, a change in use affects the building’s occupancy classification and requires a new or amended Certificate of Occupancy. Zoning regulations further determine whether residential use is permitted and under what conditions.

Recent changes have also widened the opportunity, with New York's City of Yes reforms expanding conversion eligibility to buildings constructed before 1991 in areas where residential use is permitted.

A building may look suitable on paper, but it still faces restrictions once regulations are applied. Architects and developers must navigate both what is physically achievable and what city regulations permit.

Working Within What Already Exists

The existing structure is only the starting point.

A preexisting building may make things easier to work around, but it’s naïve to think the job is half finished.

The infrastructure might help, or it might get in the way. The challenge is deciding how much of it can genuinely support the building’s new life, which must be accounted for in planning, given that it was designed for something else entirely.

Successful conversion depends on understanding both the opportunities and limitations set by the existing building. While it provides a foundation, it also defines the parameters for what is achievable.

title: Why Can One Building Have Two Architects
excerpt: People often assume the architect who designs a building oversees the project from concept through completion.
html:
People often assume the architect who designs a building oversees the project from concept through completion.

Sometimes, this isn’t the case.

Sometimes, the practice that dreams up the design isn’t the one that brings it to life.

Which sounds strange, right?

Why would a single building need two sets of architects?

The Design Architect

The building's design doesn’t appear the second the idea comes to fruition.

This responsibility falls to the design architect, who sets the project's vision and turns a client's brief into a clear concept, shaping the building's form, layout, appearance, and character.

At this stage, it’s all about what the building could become, and how to express that idea in the design.

The vision for the building is established, forming the reference point for the rest of the project, even if they aren’t the ones taking it further.

The Architect of Record

The Architect of Record is responsible for architectural delivery, building on what has been done before.

While the design concept is there, the technical details require much more, including adherence to building codes, permitting, documentation, and consultant coordination.

Drawings have to align so the structural, mechanical, and electrical systems fit within the plan. They remain involved throughout the project to address any technical questions that arise.

Simply put, their duty is to ensure the building is compliant and functional.

The building can’t be built on intent alone.

Why Separate the Two?

Not every project separates these roles. In many cases, one practice handles both.

When a project is large and complex, it creates significant demands, making it more practical to bring together practices with different strengths and specialities.

A design-led firm may be selected for its creative vision, while another firm provides the technical expertise required to advance the project through construction.

Local knowledge can be a significant advantage, especially regarding building codes, permitting, and construction standards.

A real example is 50 United Nations Plaza in New York. Foster + Partners acted as the Design Architect, while SLCE Architects served as Architect of Record.

The split went beyond job titles. Project documents gave Foster + Partners responsibility for elements of the design, including kitchen and bathroom finishes and fixtures, while SLCE retained responsibility for verifying that the design met technical and local code requirements.

This isn’t done to duplicate the work. Instead, it separates the roles so a project can combine the expertise and experience needed to deliver it.

What Does That Mean for Architectural Experience?

Architects on these projects can gain very different experience depending on which side of that relationship they work on.

Even when job titles are the same, the work can differ significantly. An architect in an AOR environment may gain experience in documentation, codes, permitting, consultant coordination, and construction-phase activities. In contrast, an architect in a design-led practice may focus on concept development, design intent, early-stage work, and client presentations.

To the public eye, both are architects. Despite the shared title, their experiences and knowledge can differ completely.

title: Why Do Data Centre Employers Keep Asking for Data Centre Experience?
excerpt: You’ve seen the news recently. It’s almost impossible to ignore at this point.
html:
You’ve seen the news recently. It’s almost impossible to ignore at this point.

Artificial intelligence is not slowing down. With every update, we see more powerful models, brand-new features and increasingly in-depth analysis. Most significantly, the technology continues to improve.

Major technology companies are competing to lead in AI development. As these models become more sophisticated, the demand for supporting infrastructure grows in parallel.

At the core of this infrastructure are data centres.

These facilities provide the computing power, storage and physical systems needed to keep AI running. As investment increases, so does the need for people who can plan, construct and deliver them.

Yet across many data centre vacancies, one requirement appears repeatedly: previous data centre experience.

Is direct experience always needed, or can skills from other complex projects be just as useful?

Why Sector Familiarity Matters

Part of the answer lies in the buildings themselves. Data centres rely on a combination of power, cooling and safety systems, all of which must be installed and tested correctly before the facility can operate. Because these systems are connected, a problem in one area can delay or disrupt the wider project.

Someone who has worked on a data centre before is more likely to understand how these projects progress, where problems usually arise and what needs to happen before the facility can go live. This level of familiarity means they can require less oversight when joining a new build, which often makes direct experience the preferred option for employers managing tight timelines and complex requirements.

However, direct data centre experience is not the only way someone can develop the skills needed to deliver complex projects.

Where Transferable Experience Fits

People working in power, pharmaceuticals, aviation or industrial construction may already be used to managing large sites, several contractors, strict safety rules and tight deadlines. Although the building itself may be different, many of the pressures are the same.

They would still need to learn the specifics of data centre project delivery and client expectations, but they are not starting from scratch. Many of the core skills are already in place. Ultimately, the key consideration is whether the role requires knowledge unique to data centres, or if broader project experience can be effectively applied.

Why the Role Changes the Answer

Data centres require a diverse range of expertise. The value of prior experience depends on the specific role being filled.

For example, a Construction Manager is responsible for coordinating the entire build. Previous experience can help them understand the order of the work, the teams involved and where delays are likely to happen. However, there may be gaps in their knowledge of how power, cooling, and testing requirements influence each stage of a data centre project.

For other positions, core skills may transfer more directly. Health and safety professionals often bring a strong understanding of risk management on construction sites. Similarly, commissioning specialists may already have experience ensuring complex systems are tested and operational before a facility opens.

Not every employer applies the same experience requirement to every vacancy. While knowledge of data centres is beneficial, many skills transfer strongly across the sector. Ultimately, it comes down to the demands of the specific role.

Matching Experience to the Position

As demand for data centres rises, so does the need for experienced professionals who can deliver these projects successfully.

Direct data centre experience remains valuable because it gives employers confidence in a candidate’s understanding of the environment, project stages, and operational pressures. That said, not every position requires the same depth of sector-specific expertise.

For some roles, experience translates well. Ultimately, the value of prior data centre experience depends on the position, its responsibilities, and how much specialist knowledge is needed from day one.

title: Why Is Power Availability Deciding Where Data Centers Get Built
excerpt: The ever-increasing demand for data center builds shows no sign of slowing, with numerous factors, most significantly Artificial Intelligence and its mass adoption.
html:
The ever-increasing demand for data center builds shows no sign of slowing, with numerous factors, most significantly Artificial Intelligence and its mass adoption.

While data centers have always been dependent on large amounts of power, this increase in pressure has only bolstered the needs of these structures.

Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimates that data centers could account for 11.8% of total U.S. electricity use by 2030.

When new developments are proposed, the planning process therefore has more to consider than before. Larger facilities require enormous blocks of capacity, and supplying that power can take years of planning, along with upgrades to the grid infrastructure needed to support it.

Power is becoming more than an operational requirement, but why is access to power such an important part of data center site selection?

What “Power Available” means

Power availability, as it sounds, is whether the amount of electricity a facility requires is available at that location by the time it needs it.

A grid connection does not guarantee that a data center will receive the power it needs. Large-scale projects may require tens or hundreds of megawatts, and local infrastructure is not always equipped to deliver that capacity.

When additional capacity is needed, utilities often must conduct grid studies and develop or upgrade new infrastructure, such as substations or transmission lines, before a site can access its full power allocation.

So while it may seem that the question is whether there is electricity nearby, it’s more about whether the site gets enough electricity when the project needs it.

Why speed to power matters

Power needs to arrive as and when a project needs it.

A development may have the land, fiber connections, and demand, yet still not have the electricity it needs to operate, and may not receive it for a number of years.

Until what is required becomes available, the data center can find itself stuck in limbo. The data center will not be able to fully operate, serve customers, or generate the revenue expected from the development.

This is why speed to power matters so much.

It’s not just about whether a site can be connected, but how quickly the connection can support the project's scale.

How does power change site selection?

Power changes site selection, as what appears to be an attractive site can just as easily be unworkable. Some of the constraints these locations create are beginning to change the geography of data center development.

Take the example of Northern Virginia, an established market, which still benefits from its enormous existing data center ecosystem. However, it’s becoming increasingly difficult to secure additional capacity, which has opened the door for other locations to compete, with greater access to land and power.

Notably, West Texas and Tennessee.

CBRE has highlighted both these locations as growing markets where energy availability is helping support new development. This shows that having the largest existing data center presence doesn’t necessarily make it the most attractive place for future development.

What Happens When the Power Isn’t There?

If the power isn’t there, then compromises have to be made, and the project needs to adapt.

The clearest option is to wait for the required grid infrastructure to be delivered. However, developers can also phase the process, bringing sections online as capacity becomes available rather than energizing the whole site at once.

To reduce the reliance on the existing grid, developers may also contribute to new infrastructure or alternative sources of generation.

If none of these options makes the project viable, then the developer has to confront the fact that the location itself may have to change.

At that point, power becomes more than what the development needs. It becomes a major influence on cost, scale, timeline, and whether the project goes ahead at all.

What Does This Mean for Development Teams?

When one of the biggest factors for the viability of a data center build comes down to power availability, planning needs to account for infrastructure much earlier in the process.

These effects are already visible in how roles within the development team are being shaped, with professionals expected to understand not only whether land can support a project, but how that site will be energized.

Staff are needed with experience managing utilities and navigating grid processes, alongside more traditional responsibilities, from permitting and entitlement to project delivery.

Data center development sits at the intersection of real estate, infrastructure and energy. Understanding these relationships makes professionals particularly valuable.
